name: Maxwell's Demon
statement: A tiny gatekeeper sorting fast molecules from slow ones seems able to create order from disorder and cheat the second law of thermodynamics.
statementAccent: create order from disorder and cheat the second law of thermodynamics
meaning: Maxwell's demon is a thought experiment devised by the physicist James Clerk Maxwell in 1867 to probe the second law of thermodynamics, which says the entropy of an isolated system never decreases. Maxwell imagined a tiny being, later called a demon, controlling a small door in a partition between two halves of a gas-filled box. By opening the door only to let fast molecules pass one way and slow molecules the other, the demon could make one side hotter and the other colder without doing any work, creating a temperature difference and so decreasing entropy, apparently violating the second law. The puzzle stood for generations: it seemed to show that intelligence or information could defeat the statistical tendency toward disorder. Its eventual resolution linked information to physics, showing that the demon's acquisition and erasure of information itself carries a thermodynamic cost.
mechanism: The demon appears to break the second law by sorting molecules using only knowledge of their speeds, spending no work yet lowering the system's entropy. The resolution, developed over the twentieth century, is that information is physical and its handling has an entropy cost. The demon must measure each molecule's speed and store that information to decide when to open the door, and its memory is finite. To keep operating it must eventually erase old information, and Landauer's principle, formulated by Rolf Landauer in 1961, states that erasing one bit of information dissipates at least kT ln 2 of energy as heat, raising the environment's entropy. Charles Bennett argued in 1982 that it is this logically irreversible erasure, not the measurement itself, that saves the second law: the entropy the demon removes from the gas is at least matched by the entropy generated in resetting its memory. Earlier, Leó Szilárd's 1929 single-molecule engine had already tied the demon's operation to information.

examples.text: The demon opens a frictionless door only for fast molecules going one way and slow ones the other, warming one chamber and cooling the other with no work done.
Erasing a single bit of information dissipates at least kT ln 2 of heat; since the demon must erase its records, this cost restores the second law.
Szilard's 1929 single-molecule version reduced the demon to a device that extracts work from one bit of information, sharpening the link between information and entropy.

variants.name: Szilard's engine
variants.text: Leó Szilárd's 1929 simplification, a one-molecule engine that converts a single bit of acquired information into work, isolating the information-entropy connection.

variants.name: The Landauer-Bennett resolution
variants.text: The account that the demon's memory erasure, costing at least kT ln 2 per bit, generates enough entropy to rescue the second law, resolving the paradox.

whyItMatters: Maxwell's demon is a landmark thought experiment that connects thermodynamics, statistical mechanics, and information theory, and its resolution helped found the physics of information. By seeming to let intelligence defeat the second law, it forced physicists to ask what entropy really is and what an observer's knowledge costs, culminating in the insight that information processing has an unavoidable thermodynamic price. Landauer's principle and Bennett's analysis of erasure turned a century-old puzzle into a cornerstone of the modern understanding that information is physical, with implications for the limits of computation and for the energy cost of erasing data. The demon thus stands not only as a classic paradox but as the seed of a deep unification between the abstract notion of information and the concrete laws of heat.

working.text: imagine a being opening a frictionless door to separate fast from slow molecules, seeming to lower entropy without doing work.
recognise that the demon must measure and remember molecular speeds, and that this information is stored in a finite physical memory.
apply Landauer's principle, that erasing each bit dissipates at least kT ln 2 of heat, so resetting the demon's memory generates the entropy that saves the second law.

limits: Maxwell's demon is a thought experiment about the foundations of the second law, not a device that can actually be built to violate it; the consensus resolution is that no such demon can produce a net decrease in total entropy once the cost of its information handling is included. The precise locus of the saving cost was debated, with earlier accounts placing it in measurement and the later Landauer-Bennett analysis placing it in irreversible erasure, and some technical discussion of the argument continues. Landauer's principle itself, while widely accepted and experimentally supported, rests on theoretical reasoning about the link between logical and thermodynamic irreversibility, so the demon remains a conceptual touchstone whose exact interpretation is still explored.
misreadings: The demon does not show the second law can be broken; properly analysed, it shows why the law holds even against an intelligent sorter, once the entropy cost of information is counted. The rescue does not come free from the mere act of observing; the modern account locates the unavoidable cost in erasing the demon's memory, per Landauer's principle, not simply in measuring. And the experiment is not a practical proposal but a probe of principle, so treating it as a blueprint for a perpetual-motion machine mistakes a puzzle designed to illuminate entropy for a design meant to defeat it.
origin: Conceived by the physicist James Clerk Maxwell in 1867 as a challenge to the second law of thermodynamics; sharpened by Leó Szilárd in 1929 and resolved through Rolf Landauer's 1961 principle and Charles Bennett's 1982 analysis of information erasure.
